claim: Mice with genetic deletion or alteration of Bad exhibit altered brain-cell fuel metabolism.
source: Mice with genetic deletion or alteration of Bad (BCL-2 agonist of cell death) exhibit altered brain-cell fuel metabolism, accompanied by resistance to acutely induced epileptic seizures; this seizure protection is mediated by ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known finding from prior work.

claim: Mice with genetic deletion or alteration of Bad exhibit resistance to acutely induced epileptic seizures.
source: Mice with genetic deletion or alteration of Bad (BCL-2 agonist of cell death) exhibit altered brain-cell fuel metabolism, accompanied by resistance to acutely induced epileptic seizures; this seizure protection is mediated by ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known finding from prior work.

claim: Seizure protection in Bad-altered mice is mediated by ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels.
source: Mice with genetic deletion or alteration of Bad (BCL-2 agonist of cell death) exhibit altered brain-cell fuel metabolism, accompanied by resistance to acutely induced epileptic seizures; this seizure protection is mediated by ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known finding from prior work.

claim: BAD's influence on neuronal KATP channels is cell-autonomous.
source: We found that BAD's influence on neuronal KATP channels was cell-autonomous and directly affected dentate granule neuron (DGN) excitability.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: BAD directly affects dentate granule neuron (DGN) excitability.
source: We found that BAD's influence on neuronal KATP channels was cell-autonomous and directly affected dentate granule neuron (DGN) excitability.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: BAD knockout reduces epileptiform activity in entorhinal-hippocampal slices.
source: BAD knockout reduced epileptiform activity, and this effect was lost upon knockout or pharmacological inhibition of KATP channels.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The effect of BAD knockout on epileptiform activity is lost upon knockout of KATP channels.
source: BAD knockout reduced epileptiform activity, and this effect was lost upon knockout or pharmacological inhibition of KATP channels.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The effect of BAD knockout on epileptiform activity is lost upon pharmacological inhibition of KATP channels.
source: BAD knockout reduced epileptiform activity, and this effect was lost upon knockout or pharmacological inhibition of KATP channels.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Targeted BAD knockout in DGNs alone is sufficient for the antiseizure effect in slices.
source: Targeted BAD knockout in DGNs alone was sufficient for the antiseizure effect in slices, consistent with a 'dentate gate' function that is reinforced by increased KATP channel activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: The antiseizure effect of targeted BAD knockout in DGNs is consistent with a 'dentate gate' function that is reinforced by increased KATP channel activity.
source: Targeted BAD knockout in DGNs alone was sufficient for the antiseizure effect in slices, consistent with a 'dentate gate' function that is reinforced by increased KATP channel activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in Figure 6, drawing on the dentate gate hypothesis.

claim: Approximately one third of epilepsy patients are resistant to pharmacological treatments.
source: Approximately one third of epilepsy patients are resistant to pharmacological treatments, and most of the current therapies can produce very severe side effects.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction without specific citation in this sentence.

claim: Most current epilepsy therapies can produce very severe side effects.
source: Approximately one third of epilepsy patients are resistant to pharmacological treatments, and most of the current therapies can produce very severe side effects.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction without specific citation in this sentence.

claim: The ketogenic diet is a very effective alternative treatment for epilepsy.
source: One very effective alternative treatment is a very low carbohydrate, high fat diet—the ketogenic diet (Hartman et al., 2007; Neal et al., 2009; Thiele, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: On a ketogenic diet, fatty acids are converted to the ketone bodies β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate.
source: On a ketogenic diet, fatty acids are converted to the ketone bodies β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate, which circulate at millimolar concentrations in the blood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ketogenic diet metabolism.

claim: Ketone bodies circulate at millimolar concentrations in the blood during a ketogenic diet.
source: On a ketogenic diet, fatty acids are converted to the ketone bodies β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate, which circulate at millimolar concentrations in the blood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ketogenic diet metabolism.

claim: Ketone bodies provide an alternative fuel to tissues, including the brain.
source: These ketone bodies provide an alternative fuel to tissues, including the brain (DeVivo et al., 1978; Mergenthaler et al., 2013; Owen et al., 1967; Zielke et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Increased ketone body metabolism produces seizure protection.
source: The observation that increased ketone body metabolism produces seizure protection suggests that fuel utilization and neuronal excitability are linked, however, the mechanisms underlying this link are poorly understood (Bough and Rho, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Fuel utilization and neuronal excitability are linked.
source: The observation that increased ketone body metabolism produces seizure protection suggests that fuel utilization and neuronal excitability are linked, however, the mechanisms underlying this link are poorly understood (Bough and Rho, 2007).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation about ketone body metabolism and seizure protection.

claim: The mechanisms underlying the link between fuel utilization and neuronal excitability are poorly understood.
source: The observation that increased ketone body metabolism produces seizure protection suggests that fuel utilization and neuronal excitability are linked, however, the mechanisms underlying this link are poorly understood (Bough and Rho, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field, supported by citation.

claim: BAD regulates both apoptosis and glucose metabolism.
source: The protein BAD (BCL-2 agonist of cell death) regulates both apoptosis and glucose metabolism (Giménez-Cassina and Danial, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: When BAD's metabolic function is disrupted by genetic alteration in mice, neurons and astrocytes display decreased glucose and increased ketone body metabolism.
source: When BAD's metabolic function is disrupted by genetic alteration in mice, neurons and astrocytes display decreased glucose and increased ketone body metabolism.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work on BAD-altered mice.

claim: Effects on brain metabolism produced by BAD alteration are reminiscent of those observed with a ketogenic diet.
source: These effects on brain metabolism produced by BAD alteration are reminiscent of those observed with a ketogenic diet.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn between BAD alteration effects and ketogenic diet effects.

claim: BAD-altered mice are strongly resistant to behavioral and electrographic seizures.
source: In fact, BAD-altered mice are also strongly resistant to behavioral and electrographic seizures.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work on BAD-altered mice.

claim: BAD modifications that decrease glucose metabolism produce a marked increase in the activity of ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels located in dentate granule neurons (DGNs).
source: At the cellular level, BAD modifications that decrease glucose metabolism produce a marked increase in the activity of ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels located in dentate granule neurons (DGNs).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work on BAD modifications.

claim: The dentate gyrus is thought to limit input into the hippocampus acting as a seizure 'gate'.
source: Thus, KATP channels in the dentate gyrus, a region that is thought to limit input into the hippocampus acting as a seizure 'gate,' are well poised to mediate the effects of BAD on DGN excitability.
evidence: This is stated as an established hypothesis in the field.

claim: KATP channels in the dentate gyrus are well poised to mediate the effects of BAD on DGN excitability.
source: Thus, KATP channels in the dentate gyrus, a region that is thought to limit input into the hippocampus acting as a seizure 'gate,' are well poised to mediate the effects of BAD on DGN excitability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location and function of KATP channels in the dentate gyrus.

claim: When KATP channels are genetically ablated, seizure resistance produced by BAD modification is abolished.
source: Indeed, when KATP channels are genetically ablated, seizure resistance produced by BAD modification is abolished (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: In BAD knockout mice, restoration of BAD expression in a fraction of DGNs allows testing whether BAD can regulate KATP channel activity in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: In BAD knockout mice, we restored BAD expression in a fraction of the DGNs, and tested individual cells to learn whether BAD could regulate KATP channel activity in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Altered KATP channel activity has consequences for excitability of individual DGNs.
source: We also tested the consequences of altered KATP channel activity for excitability of individual DGNs, which we measured using perforated patch recordings in the presence or absence of the KATP channel inhibitor glibenclamide.
evidence: This describes findings from experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: BAD ablation reduces epileptiform activity of the EC-HC circuit.
source: BAD ablation reduced the epileptiform activity of the EC-HC circuit, and this seizure-protective effect depended on the presence of functional KATP channels.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The seizure-protective effect of BAD ablation depends on the presence of functional KATP channels.
source: BAD ablation reduced the epileptiform activity of the EC-HC circuit, and this seizure-protective effect depended on the presence of functional KATP channels.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: In vitro seizure protection is reproduced by BAD deletion solely in DGNs.
source: Furthermore, this in vitro seizure protection was reproduced by BAD deletion solely in DGNs, reinforcing the notion of the dentate gyrus as a seizure gate.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: BAD deletion solely in DGNs reinforces the notion of the dentate gyrus as a seizure gate.
source: Furthermore, this in vitro seizure protection was reproduced by BAD deletion solely in DGNs, reinforcing the notion of the dentate gyrus as a seizure gate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figure 6 in the context of the dentate gate hypothesis.

claim: Bad deletion produces an increase in KATP channel activity.
source: We have previously shown that Bad deletion produces an increase in KATP channel activity (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: The increase in KATP channel activity from Bad deletion is manifested at the whole-cell level as an initial KATP conductance that gradually decreases over the first few minutes of recording after break-in.
source: This increase is manifested at the whole-cell level as an initial KATP conductance that gradually decreases over the first few minutes of recording after break-in, as the intracellular solution is dialyzed with a sufficiently high ATP concentration to inhibit the initially open KATP channels; we have called this phenomenon 'washdown' (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the 'washdown' phenomenon observed in prior work and in the current study.

claim: In wild-type DGNs, KATP channels display a very low basal open probability (NPo = 0.05%).
source: In wild-type DGNs, because KATP channels display a very low basal open probability (NPo = 0.05%), intracellular solution replacement with high ATP has no effect, so whole-cell conductance in this case remains unchanged after break-in, that is, washdown is absent in wild-type DGNs.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of wild-type DGNs based on prior knowledge.

claim: Washdown is absent in wild-type DGNs.
source: In wild-type DGNs, because KATP channels display a very low basal open probability (NPo = 0.05%), intracellular solution replacement with high ATP has no effect, so whole-cell conductance in this case remains unchanged after break-in, that is, washdown is absent in wild-type DGNs.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of wild-type DGNs based on prior knowledge and current observations.

claim: Bad−/− DGN whole-cell conductance displays a gradual decrease during the first minute after break-in and then remains unchanged.
source: Indeed, Bad−/− DGN whole-cell conductance displayed a gradual decrease during the first minute after break-in and then remained unchanged (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 1B.

claim: BAD-reconstituted Bad−/− DGNs do not display washdown.
source: In contrast, BAD-reconstituted Bad−/− DGNs did not display washdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bad−/− and BAD reconstituted Bad−/− DGNs display increases of KATP conductance of similar magnitudes with low ATP in the pipette solution.
source: Indeed, both transduced and untransduced cells displayed increases of KATP conductance of similar magnitudes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showing that the change in KATP currents is not due to a change in channel number, but rather to a change in channel open probability.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The change in KATP currents is not due to a change in channel number, but rather to a change in channel open probability.
source: Indeed, both transduced and untransduced cells displayed increases of KATP conductance of similar magnitudes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showing that the change in KATP currents is not due to a change in channel number, but rather to a change in channel open probability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bad−/− and BAD reconstituted Bad−/− DGNs are sufficiently healthy to maintain ATP levels that keep most (if not all) of their KATP channels closed.
source: This experiment also confirms that Bad−/− and BAD reconstituted Bad−/− DGNs are sufficiently healthy to maintain ATP levels that keep most (if not all) of their KATP channels closed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: BAD can modulate KATP channel activity in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: These results indicate that BAD can modulate KATP channel activity in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: Bad−/− DGNs generate fewer action potentials compared to wild-type DGNs in response to increasing current injections.
source: In response to increasing current injections, Bad−/− DGNs generated fewer action potentials compared to wild-type DGNs (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Application of glibenclamide increases excitability of Bad−/− neurons.
source: As predicted, after application of 200 nM glibenclamide, Bad−/− DGNs fired more action potentials, comparable to the response of wild-type DGNs (in the absence of glibenclamide).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 2.

claim: The number of action potentials produced by wild-type DGNs is indistinguishable in the presence or absence of glibenclamide.
source: In contrast, the number of action potentials produced by wild-type DGNs was indistinguishable in the presence or absence glibenclamide (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: KATP channels can regulate DGN excitability in an acute manner.
source: These results provide evidence that KATP channels can regulate DGN excitability in an acute manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 2.

claim: Deletion of BAD could produce seizure-protective effects by decreasing neuron excitability, via modulation of KATP channels.
source: Thus, deletion of BAD could produce seizure-protective effects by decreasing neuron excitability, via modulation of KATP channels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figure 2 and the broader context of the study.

claim: Global Bad deletion produces seizure resistance in vivo.
source: We have previously shown that global Bad deletion produces seizure resistance in vivo (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Seizure-like activity is notoriously challenging to elicit in acute slices using submersion chambers, due to lack of sufficient oxygenation.
source: Seizure-like activity is notoriously challenging to elicit in acute slices using submersion chambers, due to lack of sufficient oxygenation (Hájos et al., 2009; Hájos and Mody, 2009; Huchzermeyer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: A double perfusion chamber allows adequate oxygenation of the slice and reliably elicits seizure-like events in the presence of picrotoxin.
source: To overcome this limitation, we used a double perfusion chamber in which EC-HC slices are exposed to the extracellular solution on both sides. The flow of the oxygen-saturated extracellular solution is sufficiently high (5 ml/min) to permit an adequate oxygenation of the slice and reliably elicit seizure-like events in the presence of picrotoxin (Figure 3 and Video 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and its success in eliciting seizure-like events.

claim: Bad−/− slices spend significantly less time in SLEs compared to wild-type slices.
source: Bad−/− slices spent significantly less time in SLEs compared to wild-type slices (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The protection from picrotoxin-elicited epileptiform activity produced by BAD is abolished by genetic deletion of the pore-forming subunit of KATP channels, Kir6.2 (Kcnj11).
source: Furthermore, the protection from picrotoxin-elicited epileptiform activity produced by BAD was abolished by genetic deletion of the pore-forming subunit of KATP channels, Kir6.2 (﻿Kcnj11﻿), or by continuous application of the KATP channel inhibitor, glibenclamide (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The protection from picrotoxin-elicited epileptiform activity produced by BAD is abolished by continuous application of the KATP channel inhibitor, glibenclamide.
source: Furthermore, the protection from picrotoxin-elicited epileptiform activity produced by BAD was abolished by genetic deletion of the pore-forming subunit of KATP channels, Kir6.2 (﻿Kcnj11﻿), or by continuous application of the KATP channel inhibitor, glibenclamide (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Bad deletion prevents seizure-like activity and KATP channels acutely mediate BAD's seizure-protective effects.
source: These observations show that Bad deletion prevents seizure-like activity and that KATP channels acutely mediate BAD's seizure-protective effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 3.

claim: Long-term synaptic depression mediated by postsynaptic NMDA receptors is abolished in hippocampal slices from Bad−/− mice.
source: It has been shown that long-term synaptic depression mediated by postsynaptic NMDA receptors is abolished in hippocampal slices from Bad−/− mice (Jiao and Li, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: There are no significant differences between genotypes when KATP channels are pharmacologically inhibited or genetically deleted, confirming that genotype-specific differences in glutamatergic transmission are not affecting the seizure phenotype.
source: However, given that we observe no significant differences between the genotypes when KATP channels are pharmacologically inhibited or genetically deleted, our results confirm that any genotype-specific differences in glutamatergic transmission are not affecting the seizure phenotype we observe (see also Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figure 3, ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: A 20-fold higher picrotoxin concentration (50 µM) is needed to elicit a roughly similar epileptiform activity in adult EC-HC slices compared to juvenile slices.
source: In this case, a 20-fold higher picrotoxin concentration (50 µM) was needed to elicit a roughly similar epileptiform activity in adult EC-HC slices (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 4.

claim: Deletion of Bad protects against SLEs in adult EC-HC slices.
source: Regardless of the picrotoxin concentration needed to elicit SLEs, deletion of Bad also protected against SLEs in adult EC-HC slices.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a marked decrement in time spent in SLEs in the hippocampus of adult Bad−/− slices.
source: There was a marked decrement in time spent in SLEs in the hippocampus, though this effect was not as strong in entorhinal areas (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 4.

claim: The anti-SLE effect of BAD deletion is not as strong in entorhinal areas of adult slices.
source: There was a marked decrement in time spent in SLEs in the hippocampus, though this effect was not as strong in entorhinal areas (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 4.

claim: The dentate gyrus has been proposed to act as seizure gate, preventing epileptiform activity initiated in the EC from passing onto other hippocampal areas such as CA3 or CA1.
source: The dentate gyrus has been proposed to act as seizure gate, preventing epileptiform activity initiated in the EC from passing onto other hippocampal areas such as CA3 or CA1.
evidence: This is stated as an established hypothesis in the field.

claim: Decreasing DGN excitability alone would be sufficient to 'strengthen' the dentate gyrus' gate function, and thus decrease excitability in the EC-HC circuit.
source: Therefore, it is possible that decreasing DGN excitability alone would be sufficient to 'strengthen' the dentate gyrus' gate function, and thus decrease excitability in the EC-HC circuit responsible for many types of seizures, such as in temporal lobe epilepsy.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the dentate gate concept.

claim: Badflox/flox; Dock10-Cre mice have targeted knockout of Bad expression in the dentate gyrus but not in the rest of the hippocampus or EC.
source: These mice (Badflox/flox; Dock10-Cre) have targeted knockout of Bad expression in the dentate gyrus but not in the rest of the hippocampus or EC, as confirmed by immunostaining (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 5 and supplements.

claim: Badflox/flox; Dock10-Cre slices spend significantly less time in SLEs compared to slices from both parental lines.
source: Compared to slices from both parental lines, Badflox/flox; Dock10-Cre slices (from juvenile, P13-19, mice) spent significantly less time in SLEs (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 6.

claim: The reduction in seizure-like activity of Badflox/flox; Dock10-Cre slices that lack BAD solely in DGNs is comparable to that of Bad−/− slices.
source: Remarkably, the reduction in seizure-like activity of these slices that lack BAD solely in DGNs was comparable to that of Bad−/− slices (compare orange Badflox/flox; Dock10-Cre and green Bad−/− data in Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 6.

claim: DGN-specific BAD knockout is sufficient to produce alleviation of seizure-like activity.
source: These results demonstrate that DGN-specific BAD knockout is sufficient to produce alleviation of seizure-like activity, supporting the idea that BAD's direct action in neurons can produce seizure protection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 6.

claim: BAD's direct action in neurons can produce seizure protection.
source: These results demonstrate that DGN-specific BAD knockout is sufficient to produce alleviation of seizure-like activity, supporting the idea that BAD's direct action in neurons can produce seizure protection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 6.

claim: The results provide additional evidence to support the idea that the dentate gyrus acts as a gate for seizure activity.
source: Furthermore, the results provide additional evidence to support the idea that the dentate gyrus acts as a gate for seizure activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figure 6 in the context of the dentate gate hypothesis.

claim: Alterations in metabolism have long been proposed as avenues to treat epileptic seizures.
source: Alterations in metabolism have long been proposed as avenues to treat epileptic seizures.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The ketogenic diet has been used for almost a century as an effective treatment for epilepsy.
source: One example is the ketogenic diet, which has been used for almost a century as an effective treatment for epilepsy (Hartman et al., 2007; Neal et al., 2009; Thiele, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The switch in brain fuel metabolism from using carbohydrates to ketone bodies appears to be a major contributor to seizure protection.
source: The switch in brain fuel metabolism from using carbohydrates to ketone bodies appears to be a major contributor to seizure protection.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of evidence from ketogenic diet studies.

claim: Rats on a low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet exhibit lower glucose and increased ketone body concentrations in blood compared to control animals.
source: Compared to control animals, rats on a low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet exhibit lower glucose and increased ketone body concentrations in blood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Ketotic rats show altered brain levels of metabolites, such as the whole brain ATP/ADP ratio, suggesting an 'improved' energy state.
source: These ketotic rats show altered brain levels of metabolites, such as the whole brain ATP/ADP ratio, suggesting an 'improved' energy state (DeVivo et al., 1978).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Rats on the ketogenic diet upregulate transcripts encoding mitochondrial energy metabolism enzymes.
source: Further, rats on the ketogenic diet upregulate transcripts encoding mitochondrial energy metabolism enzymes (Bough et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Human patients undergoing treatment with a ketogenic diet show changes in brain energy metabolism in agreement with rodent studies.
source: Human patients undergoing treatment with a ketogenic diet also show changes in brain energy metabolism in agreement with rodent studies (Pan et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: The anticonvulsive effect of the ketogenic diet develops gradually over days.
source: The role of this metabolic switch in producing seizure protection is supported by the fact that although the anticonvulsive effect of the ketogenic diet develops gradually over days, it can be reversed in rodents and humans very rapidly upon carbohydrate consumption (Appleton and DeVivo, 1974; Huttenlocher, 1976; Pfeifer et al., 2008; Uhlemann and Neims, 1972).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The anticonvulsive effect of the ketogenic diet can be reversed in rodents and humans very rapidly upon carbohydrate consumption.
source: The role of this metabolic switch in producing seizure protection is supported by the fact that although the anticonvulsive effect of the ketogenic diet develops gradually over days, it can be reversed in rodents and humans very rapidly upon carbohydrate consumption (Appleton and DeVivo, 1974; Huttenlocher, 1976; Pfeifer et al., 2008; Uhlemann and Neims, 1972).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of glycolysis leads to seizure protection.
source: A different manipulation of brain metabolism by pharmacological inhibition of glycolysis also leads to seizure protection.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: The glycolytic inhibitor 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2DG) suppresses rodent seizures in vivo and in vitro through changes in gene expression related to epilepsy.
source: The glycolytic inhibitor 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2DG) suppresses rodent seizures in vivo and in vitro through changes in gene expression related to epilepsy (Garriga-Canut et al., 2006; Stafstrom et al., 2009), thus reinforcing the idea that metabolic changes can produce seizure-protective effects.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Metabolic changes can produce seizure-protective effects.
source: The glycolytic inhibitor 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2DG) suppresses rodent seizures in vivo and in vitro through changes in gene expression related to epilepsy (Garriga-Canut et al., 2006; Stafstrom et al., 2009), thus reinforcing the idea that metabolic changes can produce seizure-protective effects.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Bad−/− mice are resistant to acute seizures induced by intraperitoneal injection of kainic acid.
source: Bad−/− mice are resistant to acute seizures induced by either intraperitoneal injection of kainic acid, an agonist of a subclass of ionotropic glutamate receptors, or subcutaneous injection of pentylenetetrazole, an antagonist of GABAA receptors (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Bad−/− mice are resistant to acute seizures induced by subcutaneous injection of pentylenetetrazole.
source: Bad−/− mice are resistant to acute seizures induced by either intraperitoneal injection of kainic acid, an agonist of a subclass of ionotropic glutamate receptors, or subcutaneous injection of pentylenetetrazole, an antagonist of GABAA receptors (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: The seizure resistance produced by Bad deletion can be effective in different types of epilepsy.
source: Because these two pharmacologic models of status epilepticus act through different mechanisms, producing seizures with different characteristics, indicating that the seizure resistance produced by Bad deletion can be effective in different types of epilepsy.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Bad deletion protects against seizures induced by different mechanisms.

claim: Bad deletion can reduce seizures and increase longevity in a genetic mouse model of epilepsy and sudden unexplained death in epilepsy.
source: We have also shown that Bad deletion can reduce seizures and increase longevity in a genetic mouse model of epilepsy and sudden unexplained death in epilepsy (Foley et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: The switch between the apoptotic and metabolic roles of BAD occurs through phosphorylation of its serine 155.
source: The switch between the apoptotic and metabolic roles of BAD occurs through phosphorylation of its serine 155 (equivalent to serine 118 in human BAD) (Danial et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Serine 155 phosphorylation enhances glucose metabolism while inhibiting BAD's apoptotic function.
source: Serine 155 phosphorylation enhances glucose metabolism while inhibiting BAD's apoptotic function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about BAD function.

claim: Mutation of serine 155 to a non-phosphorylatable alanine (BadS155A) phenocopies the glucose-to-ketone-body fuel switch in BAD knockout neurons and astrocytes.
source: Mutation of this residue to a non-phosphorylatable alanine (BadS155A) phenocopies the glucose-to-ketone-body fuel switch in BAD knockout neurons and astrocytes, and also produces in vivo seizure protection (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: BadS155A mutation produces in vivo seizure protection.
source: Mutation of this residue to a non-phosphorylatable alanine (BadS155A) phenocopies the glucose-to-ketone-body fuel switch in BAD knockout neurons and astrocytes, and also produces in vivo seizure protection (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Both Bad−/− and BadS155A have the same effects on KATP channel activity and seizure protection.
source: Because both Bad−/− and BadS155A have the same effects on KATP channel activity and seizure protection, but have opposite effects on apoptosis, the effects of BAD knockout on seizure-like activity are very likely due to BAD's effect on metabolism and not on apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between Bad−/− and BadS155A effects.

claim: Bad−/− and BadS155A have opposite effects on apoptosis.
source: Because both Bad−/− and BadS155A have the same effects on KATP channel activity and seizure protection, but have opposite effects on apoptosis, the effects of BAD knockout on seizure-like activity are very likely due to BAD's effect on metabolism and not on apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between Bad−/− and BadS155A effects.

claim: The effects of BAD knockout on seizure-like activity are very likely due to BAD's effect on metabolism and not on apoptosis.
source: Because both Bad−/− and BadS155A have the same effects on KATP channel activity and seizure protection, but have opposite effects on apoptosis, the effects of BAD knockout on seizure-like activity are very likely due to BAD's effect on metabolism and not on apoptosis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison between Bad−/− and BadS155A effects.

claim: Knockout of BIM or PUMA leads to neuroprotection related to seizures.
source: Knockout of BIM or PUMA leads to neuroprotection related to seizures (Engel et al., 2011, 2010; Murphy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Ablation of BIM or PUMA is not seizure protective immediately after kainic acid injection.
source: However, in contrast to our previous observations of seizure protection by BAD deletion (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012), ablation of BIM or PUMA is not seizure protective immediately after kainic acid injection (Engel et al., 2010; Murphy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: BIM and PUMA promote hippocampal neuron death in a model of chronic seizures.
source: Instead, these other BCL-2 family members, promote hippocampal neuron death in a model of chronic seizures (intra-amygdala microinjection of kainic acid), thus, Bim−/− or Puma−/− animals exhibit long-term seizure protection due to decreased cell death, as opposed to Bad−/− mice that are resistant to acute seizures due to a switch in fuel preference.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work.

claim: Bim−/− or Puma−/− animals exhibit long-term seizure protection due to decreased cell death.
source: Instead, these other BCL-2 family members, promote hippocampal neuron death in a model of chronic seizures (intra-amygdala microinjection of kainic acid), thus, Bim−/− or Puma−/− animals exhibit long-term seizure protection due to decreased cell death, as opposed to Bad−/− mice that are resistant to acute seizures due to a switch in fuel preference.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work.

claim: Bad−/− mice are resistant to acute seizures due to a switch in fuel preference.
source: Instead, these other BCL-2 family members, promote hippocampal neuron death in a model of chronic seizures (intra-amygdala microinjection of kainic acid), thus, Bim−/− or Puma−/− animals exhibit long-term seizure protection due to decreased cell death, as opposed to Bad−/− mice that are resistant to acute seizures due to a switch in fuel preference.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the mechanism of seizure protection in Bad−/− mice.

claim: The metabolic shift produced by BAD knockout leads to an increase in KATP channel activity.
source: The metabolic shift produced by BAD knockout leads to an increase in KATP channel activity.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work and the current study.

claim: In cell-attached recordings from DGNs, the open probability of KATP channels is markedly increased in Bad−/− cells compared to wild-type cells.
source: In cell-attached recordings from DGNs, where the intracellular medium—and thus ATP—is undisturbed, the open probability of KATP channels is markedly increased in Bad−/− cells compared to wild-type cells, where these channels are mostly closed (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: The extra whole-cell conductance due to increased KATP channel activity in Bad−/− DGNs can be seen to disappear as the intracellular medium is dialyzed with an elevated ATP concentration.
source: Furthermore, the extra whole-cell conductance due to this increased KATP channel activity in Bad−/− DGNs can be seen to disappear as the intracellular medium is dialyzed with an elevated ATP concentration (Figure 1), an effect absent in wild-type DGNs (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 1 and prior work.

claim: The altered KATP conductance is due to the change in open probability and not to a change in the number of functional KATP channels.
source: The altered KATP conductance is due to the change in open probability and not to a change in the number of functional KATP channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In whole-cell experiments with low ATP in the intracellular medium, the maximal conductance measured after disinhibition of the channels is very similar in wild-type and Bad−/− DGNs.
source: In whole-cell experiments with low ATP in the intracellular medium, the maximal conductance measured after disinhibition of the channels is very similar in wild-type and Bad−/− DGNs (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012) and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and prior work.

claim: KATP channels are required for the anti-seizure effect of Bad deletion.
source: Furthermore, KATP channels are required for the anti-seizure effect of Bad deletion.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from prior work and the current study.

claim: There is a reversal of seizure protection in Bad−/− mice upon further deletion of Kcnj11 (Kir6.2).
source: There is a reversal of seizure protection in Bad−/− mice upon further deletion of Kcnj11 (Kir6.2), the pore-forming subunit of neuronal KATP channels (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: The susceptibility of Bad−/−; Kcnj11−/− double knockout mice to kainic acid induced seizures is comparable to that of wild-type mice.
source: More specifically, the susceptibility of Bad−/−; Kcnj11−/− double knockout mice to kainic acid induced seizures is comparable to that of wild-type mice, providing compelling evidence that KATP channels are required for BAD-mediated seizure resistance.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work.

claim: KATP channels have been seen to affect neuronal excitability.
source: Previously, KATP channels have been seen to affect neuronal excitability (Allen and Brown, 2004; Haller et al., 2001; Pierrefiche et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: KATP channels link metabolism to excitability because they are inhibited by intracellular ATP, and activated by intracellular ADP.
source: KATP channels link metabolism to excitability because they are inhibited by intracellular ATP, and activated by intracellular ADP (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1998; Nichols, 2006; Proks and Ashcroft, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: KATP channels are widely expressed in the brain.
source: They are also widely expressed in the brain (Dunn-Meynell et al., 1998; Liss and Roeper, 2001) and are present at a particularly high density in DGNs (Karschin et al., 1997; Mourre et al., 1991; Zawar et al., 1999), where their single-channel activity can be readily recorded (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012; Pelletier et al., 2000; Tanner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: KATP channels are present at a particularly high density in DGNs.
source: They are also widely expressed in the brain (Dunn-Meynell et al., 1998; Liss and Roeper, 2001) and are present at a particularly high density in DGNs (Karschin et al., 1997; Mourre et al., 1991; Zawar et al., 1999), where their single-channel activity can be readily recorded (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012; Pelletier et al., 2000; Tanner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The regulation of neuronal excitability by KATP channels has been extensively studied in the context of protection from hypoxia or ischemia.
source: The regulation of neuronal excitability by KATP channels has been extensively studied in the context of protection from hypoxia or ischemia: these channels prevent prolonged depolarizations that produce neuronal damage (Sun and Feng, 2013; Sun et al., 2006; Yamada et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: KATP channels prevent prolonged depolarizations that produce neuronal damage during hypoxia or ischemia.
source: The regulation of neuronal excitability by KATP channels has been extensively studied in the context of protection from hypoxia or ischemia: these channels prevent prolonged depolarizations that produce neuronal damage (Sun and Feng, 2013; Sun et al., 2006; Yamada et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: KATP channels are crucial in the response of hypothalamic neurons to circulating glucose levels.
source: Additionally, they are crucial in the response of hypothalamic neurons to circulating glucose levels (Ashford et al., 1990; Levin, 2002; Miki et al., 2001; Rowe et al., 1996; Song et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: KATP channels can acutely modulate DGN excitability at the cellular level.
source: Our results show that KATP channels can acutely modulate DGN excitability at the cellular level (Figure 2) as well as network excitability in slices that are disinhibited by picrotoxin to exhibit seizure-like events (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: KATP channels can acutely modulate network excitability in slices that are disinhibited by picrotoxin to exhibit seizure-like events.
source: Our results show that KATP channels can acutely modulate DGN excitability at the cellular level (Figure 2) as well as network excitability in slices that are disinhibited by picrotoxin to exhibit seizure-like events (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Acute pharmacological reversal of DGN excitability supports the role of neuronal KATP channels as key molecules mediating seizure protection.
source: This acute pharmacological reversal of DGN excitability supports the role of neuronal KATP channels as key molecules mediating seizure protection (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012; Yamada et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figure 2, supported by citations.

claim: Eliminating Bad specifically in the brain can lead to changes in KATP channel activity and network excitability.
source: We also show that eliminating Bad specifically in the brain can lead to changes in KATP channel activity and network excitability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 1 and 6.

claim: When BAD was restored in single Bad−/− DGNs via AAV, KATP channel activity reverted to that of wild-type DGNs.
source: When BAD was restored in single Bad−/− DGNs via AAV, KATP channel activity reverted to that of wild-type DGNs (Figure 1), signifying that BAD's effect on neurons can be reversed in a cell-autonomous manner and does not seem to depend on other types of brain cells, such as astrocytes.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 1.

claim: BAD's effect on neurons can be reversed in a cell-autonomous manner and does not seem to depend on other types of brain cells, such as astrocytes.
source: When BAD was restored in single Bad−/− DGNs via AAV, KATP channel activity reverted to that of wild-type DGNs (Figure 1), signifying that BAD's effect on neurons can be reversed in a cell-autonomous manner and does not seem to depend on other types of brain cells, such as astrocytes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figure 1.

claim: Either global knockout or DGN-targeted knockout of BAD produces a decrease in picrotoxin-induced seizure-like activity.
source: At the network level, we show that either global knockout or DGN-targeted knockout of BAD produced a decrease in picrotoxin-induced seizure-like activity (Figures 3 and 6), and this effect was mediated by KATP channels.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: The decrease in picrotoxin-induced seizure-like activity from BAD knockout is mediated by KATP channels.
source: At the network level, we show that either global knockout or DGN-targeted knockout of BAD produced a decrease in picrotoxin-induced seizure-like activity (Figures 3 and 6), and this effect was mediated by KATP channels.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: BAD's action in specific neuronal populations may alleviate seizures.
source: This suggests that BAD's action in specific neuronal populations may alleviate seizures.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figure 6.

claim: It is yet to be tested whether Bad deletion solely in DGNs produces seizure protection in vivo.
source: However, it is yet to be tested whether Bad deletion solely in DGNs produces seizure protection in vivo.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap and future direction.

claim: Future in vivo studies involving targeted Bad deletion in different neuron populations are needed to pinpoint whether additional brain regions are necessary for the BAD-mediated antiseizure effect.
source: Future in vivo studies involving targeted Bad deletion in different neuron populations are needed to pinpoint whether additional brain regions are necessary for the BAD-mediated antiseizure effect.
evidence: This identifies a future direction for research.

claim: The KATP-mediated decrease in DGN excitability elicited inhibition of network excitability, consistent with the seizure protection observed in BAD-altered mice.
source: The KATP-mediated decrease in DGN excitability elicited inhibition of network excitability, consistent with the seizure protection observed in BAD-altered mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 2, 3, and 6.

claim: The dentate gyrus controls the input from the entorhinal cortex into the rest of the hippocampus.
source: The dentate gyrus controls the input from the entorhinal cortex into the rest of the hippocampus; ictal activity can be initiated in the EC and propagate through the dentate gyrus to CA3 and/or CA1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about dentate gyrus function.

claim: Ictal activity can be initiated in the EC and propagate through the dentate gyrus to CA3 and/or CA1.
source: The dentate gyrus controls the input from the entorhinal cortex into the rest of the hippocampus; ictal activity can be initiated in the EC and propagate through the dentate gyrus to CA3 and/or CA1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about seizure propagation.

claim: Because of the recurrent connectivity of the EC-HP circuit due to the afferents from CA1 to the EC that pass through the subiculum, excitation can re-enter the EC.
source: Furthermore, because of the recurrent connectivity of the EC-HP circuit due to the afferents from CA1 to the EC that pass through the subiculum, excitation can then re-enter the EC (Andersen et al., 1966; Barbarosie et al., 2000; Barbarosie and Avoli, 1997; Behr et al., 1998; Spencer and Spencer, 1994; Uva et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about EC-HP circuit connectivity, supported by citations.

claim: The effect of the dentate gate may be observed by decreased excitation not only throughout the hippocampus but also extending to the EC.
source: In this way, the effect of the dentate gate in principle may be observed by decreased excitation not only throughout the hippocampus but also extending to the EC, as we observe in this study.
evidence: This is an inference about how the dentate gate function manifests in the data.

claim: Limiting DGN excitability could lead to seizure protection by 'strengthening' the dentate gate.
source: Thus, limiting DGN excitability could lead to seizure protection by 'strengthening' the dentate gate.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of seizure protection.

claim: Ictal activity could directly propagate from the EC to CA1.
source: It has also been observed that ictal activity could either directly propagate from the EC to CA1 (Ang et al., 2006) or originate in the dentate and subsequently spread to the EC (Lu et al., 2016; Meyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Ictal activity could originate in the dentate and subsequently spread to the EC.
source: It has also been observed that ictal activity could either directly propagate from the EC to CA1 (Ang et al., 2006) or originate in the dentate and subsequently spread to the EC (Lu et al., 2016; Meyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: BAD-dependent decrease in time spent in SLEs is consistent with the dentate gate hypothesis.
source: Our observations of a BAD-dependent decrease in time spent in SLEs are consistent with this picture (Figures 3, 4 and 6).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figures 3, 4, and 6 in the context of the dentate gate hypothesis.

claim: Bad deletion specific to the dentate is sufficient to elicit protection from picrotoxin-triggered SLEs.
source: Further, we found that Bad deletion specific to the dentate was sufficient to elicit protection from picrotoxin-triggered SLEs.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 6.

claim: EC-HC slices from mice lacking BAD exclusively in DGNs display a similar reduction in seizure-like activity to that of slices from mice in which BAD had been globally knocked-out.
source: Remarkably, EC-HC slices from mice lacking BAD exclusively in DGNs displayed a similar reduction in seizure-like activity to that of slices from mice in which BAD had been globally knocked-out (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 6.

claim: Immunostaining results show robust BAD knockout in DGNs of Badflox/flox; Dock10-Cre mice compared to the parental controls.
source: Our immunostaining results show robust BAD knockout in DGNs (including stratum lucidum, which contains the mossy fiber projections from DGNs) of Badflox/flox; Dock10-Cre mice compared to the parental controls (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 5.

claim: Targeted Bad knockout has no discernable effect on BAD expression elsewhere in the brain slices examined.
source: This targeted Bad knockout had no discernable effect on BAD expression elsewhere in the brain slices we examined.
evidence: This is a finding from the immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 5 and supplements.

claim: The absence of Bad throughout the DGN layer of Badflox/flox; Dock10-Cre mice, together with the substantial effect on the seizure-like activity, is most consistent with a primary effect of the dentate acting as a seizure gate.
source: We cannot rule out that very sparse expression of Dock10-Cre in the EC (Allen Institute Mouse Brain Atlas; expression of Dock10) could affect some cells, however, the absence of Bad throughout the DGN layer of Badflox/flox; Dock10-Cre mice, together with the substantial effect on the seizure-like activity, seems most consistent with a primary effect of the dentate acting as a seizure gate, as suggested previously from both in vitro and in vivo experiments (Dengler and Coulter, 2016; Heinemann et al., 1992; Hsu, 2007; Krook-Magnuson et al., 2015; 2013; Lothman et al., 1992).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figures 5 and 6, supported by citations.

claim: Seizure-like activity is decreased in all areas (including EC) of the EC-HC slices upon BAD knockout specifically in DGNs.
source: Interestingly, seizure-like activity is decreased in all areas (including EC) of the EC-HC slices upon BAD knockout specifically in DGNs; as previously mentioned this could reflect the recurrent nature of the EC-HC circuit where the dentate gate could decrease reentrant excitation into the EC.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 6.

claim: The decrease in seizure-like activity in all areas upon DGN-specific BAD knockout could reflect the recurrent nature of the EC-HC circuit where the dentate gate could decrease reentrant excitation into the EC.
source: Interestingly, seizure-like activity is decreased in all areas (including EC) of the EC-HC slices upon BAD knockout specifically in DGNs; as previously mentioned this could reflect the recurrent nature of the EC-HC circuit where the dentate gate could decrease reentrant excitation into the EC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figure 6.

claim: These observations illuminate a mechanism by which neuronal metabolism can regulate neuronal excitability to produce seizure protection.
source: Taken together, these observations illuminate a mechanism by which neuronal metabolism can regulate neuronal excitability to produce seizure protection.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from all the data in the study.

claim: Mechanisms of both seizure production and seizure protection appear to change throughout brain development.
source: Mechanisms of both seizure production and seizure protection appear to change throughout brain development (Dengler and Coulter, 2016; Holmes and Ben-Ari, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: A 20-fold higher picrotoxin concentration is required to elicit robust SLEs in adult slices compared to juvenile.
source: Consistent with this, we observed that a 20-fold higher picrotoxin concentration is required to elicit robust SLEs in adult slices compared to juvenile (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the juvenile mouse brain, most DGNs are immature and still integrating into the circuit.
source: In the juvenile mouse brain, most DGNs are immature and still integrating into the circuit; they are more excitable than mature cells and have yet to fully develop their inhibitory connections (Espósito et al., 2005; Mongiat and Schinder, 2011; Piatti et al., 2013; Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Juvenile DGNs are more excitable than mature cells and have yet to fully develop their inhibitory connections.
source: In the juvenile mouse brain, most DGNs are immature and still integrating into the circuit; they are more excitable than mature cells and have yet to fully develop their inhibitory connections (Espósito et al., 2005; Mongiat and Schinder, 2011; Piatti et al., 2013; Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The results are consistent with developmental changes in GABAergic signaling, including the shift from a depolarizing to a hyperpolarizing chloride current during brain maturation.
source: Our results are also consistent with developmental changes in GABAergic signaling, including the shift from a depolarizing to a hyperpolarizing chloride current during brain maturation (Ben-Ari et al., 2012; Hollrigel et al., 1998; Liu et al., 1996; Rheims et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: In adults, BAD-mediated seizure resistance is more limited to the hippocampal region and is not as prominent in the EC.
source: We also observed that in adults, BAD-mediated seizure resistance is more limited to the hippocampal region and is not as prominent in the EC (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 4.

claim: The pattern of BAD-mediated seizure resistance in adults is consistent with BAD-mediated reinforcement of a dentate gate that limits invasion of elevated EC activity into the hippocampus.
source: This pattern is consistent with BAD-mediated reinforcement of a dentate gate that limits invasion of elevated EC activity into the hippocampus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figure 4.

claim: In juvenile slices, DGN-specific deletion of BAD affects EC activity, which may indicate that at lower levels of disinhibition, recurrent excitation from the hippocampus to EC is more relevant than in adult slices.
source: The fact that in juvenile slices, DGN-specific deletion of BAD also affected EC activity may indicate that, at the lower levels of disinhibition (lower [picrotoxin]), recurrent excitation from the hippocampus to EC is more relevant than in adult slices.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data comparing juvenile and adult slices.

claim: The detailed mechanism by which BAD knockout influences KATP channel activity is still unknown.
source: The detailed mechanism by which BAD knockout influences KATP channel activity is still unknown.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: One possibility is that the ATP concentration in a compartment local to the channels is reduced in Bad−/− mice.
source: One possibility is that although ATP in the whole brain of Bad−/− mice is not reduced (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012), the ATP concentration in a compartment local to the channels is reduced.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism.

claim: ATP consumption at the plasma membrane by the Na+/K+ pump can increase KATP channel opening.
source: Indeed, ATP consumption at the plasma membrane by the Na+/K+ pump can increase KATP channel opening (Haller et al., 2001; Tanner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Glycolytic enzymes are associated with membrane proteins.
source: Further, glycolytic enzymes are associated with membrane proteins (Dhar-Chowdhury et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2001; Mercer and Dunham, 1981; Paul et al., 1979) and have been found to form a complex with KATP channels (Dhar-Chowdhury et al., 2005; Dubinsky et al., 1998; Hong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Glycolytic enzymes have been found to form a complex with KATP channels.
source: Further, glycolytic enzymes are associated with membrane proteins (Dhar-Chowdhury et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2001; Mercer and Dunham, 1981; Paul et al., 1979) and have been found to form a complex with KATP channels (Dhar-Chowdhury et al., 2005; Dubinsky et al., 1998; Hong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Glycolytic inhibition by application of 2DG produces a decrease in cellular and network excitability mediated by KATP channels and an increase of GABAergic tonic inhibition through neurosteroids.
source: Glycolytic inhibition by application of 2DG produces a decrease in cellular and network excitability mediated by KATP channels and an increase of GABAergic tonic inhibition through neurosteroids (Forte et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: A direct interaction between BAD and the glycolytic enzyme hexokinase has not been studied.
source: Even though a direct interaction between BAD and the glycolytic enzyme hexokinase has not been studied, BAD interacts with glucokinase (hexokinase IV) in pancreatic β-cells and hepatocytes (Danial et al., 2008, 2003; Giménez-Cassina et al., 2014), and thus, could be affecting glycolytic ATP production through this interaction.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: BAD interacts with glucokinase (hexokinase IV) in pancreatic β-cells and hepatocytes.
source: Even though a direct interaction between BAD and the glycolytic enzyme hexokinase has not been studied, BAD interacts with glucokinase (hexokinase IV) in pancreatic β-cells and hepatocytes (Danial et al., 2008, 2003; Giménez-Cassina et al., 2014), and thus, could be affecting glycolytic ATP production through this interaction.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: BAD could be affecting glycolytic ATP production through interaction with glucokinase.
source: Even though a direct interaction between BAD and the glycolytic enzyme hexokinase has not been studied, BAD interacts with glucokinase (hexokinase IV) in pancreatic β-cells and hepatocytes (Danial et al., 2008, 2003; Giménez-Cassina et al., 2014), and thus, could be affecting glycolytic ATP production through this interaction.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism.

claim: Metabolites other than ATP, such as PIP2, also regulate KATP channels.
source: Metabolites other than ATP, such as PIP2, also regulate KATP channels (Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017; Shyng et al., 2000; Shyng and Nichols, 1998), and Bad deletion might modify the properties of KATP channels by altering PIP2 or through other mechanisms, such as phosphorylation (Béguin et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Bad deletion might modify the properties of KATP channels by altering PIP2 or through other mechanisms, such as phosphorylation.
source: Metabolites other than ATP, such as PIP2, also regulate KATP channels (Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017; Shyng et al., 2000; Shyng and Nichols, 1998), and Bad deletion might modify the properties of KATP channels by altering PIP2 or through other mechanisms, such as phosphorylation (Béguin et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: KATP channels can acutely regulate cellular and network excitability.
source: We have shown that KATP channels can acutely regulate cellular and network excitability, but whether BAD manipulation itself can affect excitability in an acute manner remains an open question.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Whether BAD manipulation itself can affect excitability in an acute manner remains an open question.
source: We have shown that KATP channels can acutely regulate cellular and network excitability, but whether BAD manipulation itself can affect excitability in an acute manner remains an open question.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap and future direction.

claim: Inhibitory molecules of BAD's glycolytic role would be valuable to learn the time course by which BAD manipulation exerts its effect on KATP channels, and thus, seizure protection.
source: Inhibitory molecules of BAD's glycolytic role would be valuable to learn the time course by which BAD manipulation exerts its effect on KATP channels, and thus, seizure protection.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Because KATP channels regulate a wide variety of processes in the brain, targeting the mechanisms that link the BAD-induced change in metabolism to excitability might prove a better pharmacological strategy than targeting neuronal KATP channels.
source: Because KATP channels regulate a wide variety of processes in the brain, targeting the (still unknown) mechanisms that link the BAD-induced change in metabolism to excitability might prove a better pharmacological strategy than targeting neuronal KATP channels.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future therapeutic development.

claim: Mimicking the effect of BAD knockout on fuel preference using small molecules could be a valuable avenue for development of new epilepsy therapies.
source: Mimicking the effect of BAD knockout on fuel preference using small molecules could be a valuable avenue for development of new epilepsy therapies.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future therapeutic development.
